title: Semivariance and Semivolatility in Portfolio Selection: A Unified Framework for Downside-Risk Portfolio Models
summary: In this paper, we study downside risk in portfolio selection beyond minimum-risk models, where semivariance and its square root, semivolatility, yield the same portfolio. Downside-risk models are often presented as direct extensions of their variance-based counterparts, although different classes of portfolio problems require different properties of the risk measure. We classify these models by the degree of positive homogeneity of the risk measure in the weights: degree one makes risk contributions add up to the portfolio risk and keeps diversification and reward-to-risk ratios scale invariant. For three thresholds, the portfolio mean, zero and a market-index return, we state a non-degeneracy condition on long-only downside risk under which the risk-parity, most-diversified and Sortino-ratio problems are well posed. Under this condition, the two ratio problems reduce to convex programs, and the differentiability of semivolatility ensures that the risk-budgeting formulation attains the prescribed budgets. We also characterize when below-mean semivolatility is additive. Finally, we provide an out-of-sample analysis on two real-world datasets of total returns, the current constituents of the Dow Jones and Nasdaq-100 indexes. We compare seventeen long-only strategies, covering the minimum-risk, reward-to-risk, risk-parity and most-diversified families, in a rolling-window backtest, and test the differences within each family by block-bootstrap inference.

title: Dynamic stochastic multi-attribute group decision-making based on fractional-order stochastic dominance criteria
summary: The stochastic dominance criterion has been widely employed in stochastic multi-attribute decision making as a robust tool for quantitatively comparing decision-makers' preferences over alternatives. Existing research predominantly relies on integer-order stochastic dominance criteria within static modeling frameworks. However, the integer-order scale is often too coarse, and real-world decision-making typically occurs in dynamic environments, for which static methods are inadequate. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel dynamic stochastic multi-attribute group decision making model based on fractional-order stochastic dominance criteria. In this model, we introduce the priority degree under fractional-order stochastic dominance, which not only encompasses the priority degree under integer-order stochastic dominance, but also is applicable to decision-makers whose utility functions are not concave everywhere. Consequently, the proposed model captures the dominance relations between alternatives with greater accuracy and flexibility. Moreover, the model allows for the addition or removal of attributes and alternatives across decision periods, thereby exhibiting the applicability to any dynamic decision process. Numerical examples and comparative analyses show the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach, highlighting its broader applicability compared with conventional methods. This study enriches the theoretical foundation of dynamic stochastic multi-attribute group decision making and contributes to improving the reliability and precision of decision outcomes.

title: Pretrained Tabular Features and the Measurement of Financial Proximity
summary: Spatial arbitrage pricing theory (S-APT) extends factor models to allow returns to spill over between connected firms, beyond what common risk factors explain. In recent years, tabular foundation models (TFMs) have matched or outperformed tuned gradient-boosted and bagged ensembles on small and medium-sized tabular benchmarks. Although their predictive performance is strong, these models reveal little about what they have learned, which limits their use in regulated financial applications that require explanation. Internal representations are widely used to probe what neural networks learn and to measure similarity. In this paper, we use the frozen representations of four TFMs as a measure of financial dissimilarity in a spatial asset-pricing model of US equities from 2011 to 2025, and find that their estimated gains over a direct distance between the same disclosures become consistently positive once broad SEC filing data are included. This reframes tabular foundation models from black-box predictors into instruments for measuring economic structure, with immediate applications to peer selection, risk attribution and network-based asset pricing. More broadly, our findings suggest that the internal representations of foundation models, not only their predictions, deserve study as economic objects, opening a new line of research on what pretrained models know about firms.

title: Burning the Bridge: Agentification and Domestic Value Added
summary: Firms that replace local work with foreign AI agents can produce more per paid hour while generating less income at home. We study this trade-off in a small open economy where exporters and local services both use agents. Once wages reach a reservation floor, extending agent use in local services lowers domestic income at unchanged foreign costs. Value added at constant prices and consumption also fall if suppliers capture enough of the saving. Exporters have an offset: adopting agents can expand production and earn the foreign exchange needed to pay for them. The difference is substantial. Using Brazilian accounts as a reference, a supplier bargaining share above about 0.15 is sufficient to make further local-service adoption reduce value added even at negligible foreign costs. The corresponding threshold in tradables is about 0.66. We derive separate export-growth requirements for preserving income and consumption and illustrate them using historical accounts for Brazil and Mexico. Cheaper agents ease the consumption requirement; lower export prices raise it. Over time, declining domestic capabilities can also make returning to local production more expensive, allowing suppliers to charge more at renewal.

title: The Effect of Remote Working on Regional Waste: Evidence from South Korea
summary: Remote working, or work-from-home (WFH), has become common around the world. However, its broader effects on social welfare, including waste generation, remain understudied. This study examines the impact of remote work on regional waste production in South Korea, using the COVID-19 pandemic as a natural experiment. Overall household waste changed little, but regions with greater WFH eligibility saw increases in plastic and textile waste and a decrease in food waste. These findings suggest that remote work may change consumption patterns and daily routines. Understanding these effects can help inform sustainable work practices and waste management as remote work becomes more widespread.

title: Grokipedia stretches the US political spectrum
summary: Language models now write reference works that people and other AI systems consult. Grokipedia, written by xAI's model, presents itself as a less biased alternative to crowd-edited Wikipedia. We compare the biographies of 1,614 Democratic and Republican current and former politicians, from Andrew Jackson to members of the current Congress, on both encyclopedias in February and November 2026. For nine in ten Republicans, Grokipedia's biography reads as if written by a more conservative author than Wikipedia's. For Democrats, this holds only about half the time. We find the politicians' ideology explains this asymmetry. For 1,022 politicians with Congressional roll call voting records, how conservative the author seems rises linearly with the politician's ideology and about twice as steeply on Grokipedia as on Wikipedia. Republicans in races where Elon Musk's America PAC spent money show no extra bias. Rather than favoring a party, Grokipedia stretches the political spectrum, moving the biographies of the most liberal politicians further left and of the most conservative politicians further right.
